opus-5.5.text:
I think the thing I'm most excited about is moving from AI that can solve problems we already know how to pose to AI that can come up with the problems themselves. A lot of what we've seen so far, even in really impressive results like competition math, is the model taking a well-specified question and finding a path to the answer. That's hard and it's genuinely creative in places. You see proofs where the model tries something unexpected and it works. But the deeper kind of originality in science is knowing which question is worth asking.

If you look at the history of mathematics, many of the biggest leaps weren't just clever solutions. Someone said, "Here's a new object worth studying," or "Here's a way of looking at this old area that makes everything simpler." Think of defining a new structure, or connecting two fields nobody thought were related. That's taste. It's judgment about what's interesting and fruitful, and it's much harder to measure than whether you got the right answer.

So what I'd love to see next is models that can sustain long stretches of open-ended research: forming conjectures, testing them, throwing out the ones that don't pan out, and eventually landing on something a human expert reads and says, "I wouldn't have thought of that, and it's clearly important." Not just a surprising answer, but a surprising direction.

Part of getting there is technical. We need models that can reason for much longer, verify their own work, and handle tasks where there isn't a clean reward signal at the end. Part of it is learning how to collaborate. I think the first real instances of this kind of originality will probably come from a researcher and a model working together, where the model is a genuine intellectual partner rather than just a tool. That's the moment I'm looking forward to.

r001.rationale: The response expresses interest in models originating research questions and directions, but it does not say they should create ideas from scratch rather than recombine existing ideas. It even gives connecting two fields as an example.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: That's a question I think about a lot, actually. When we got the gold medal result on the IMO, the thing that struck me wasn't just that the model solved the problems. It was that some of the proofs took routes a human competitor probably wouldn't have taken. Not better, necessarily, but different. And that's a small taste of what I'd like to see more of.

The originality I really want is the kind where a model doesn't just answer a question we pose, but notices that the question is slightly wrong, or that there's a more interesting question sitting next to it. In math research, the hard part is often not proving the theorem. It's figuring out which theorem is worth proving, and which definitions make the whole thing fall out cleanly. That taste, that sense of "this is the right object to look at," is something we haven't really seen from models yet in a convincing way.

So concretely, I'd love to see a model pose a conjecture that a working mathematician looks at and says, "Huh, I hadn't thought of that, and it's actually interesting." Not a rediscovery, and not a recombination of known patterns, but something with a bit of a surprise in it. And then ideally the model can go and make progress on it, and be honest about where it gets stuck.

The honesty part matters to me. Originality without calibration is just noise. Anyone can generate a thousand wild ideas. The valuable thing is generating a few that are genuinely new and knowing which ones those are. I think the next big step is models that can do both at once: be creative at the level of problem selection, and rigorous enough to know when they've actually found something.

r001.rationale: The guest wants models to produce genuinely new, surprising conjectures and explicitly distinguishes that from rediscovering or recombining known patterns.

astra-6.text:
I’d like to see AI come up with a useful idea that we didn’t think to ask for. There’s a kind of originality in solving a problem someone gives you, but there’s another kind in noticing that there’s an interesting problem in the first place. Why is this pattern showing up? Is there a simpler way to understand it? Could these two ideas be connected?

And I’d want it to follow through—to test the idea, find where it breaks, and refine it. Something surprising is a starting point. Something surprising that holds up under scrutiny and helps us understand more would be really exciting.

r001.rationale: The candidate wants AI to notice useful, unasked questions and develop them, but does not express a preference for ideas originated from scratch over recombining ideas from different fields. Its mention of connecting ideas does not establish that contrast.

sol-6.1.text: I’d love to see AI come up with a new way of thinking about a problem, rather than just solve a problem we already know how to formulate. In math, that could mean noticing a connection between two areas that seem unrelated, or proposing a definition that makes a whole set of questions easier to understand. A really exciting result would be something surprising at first, but that people can then build on—something that changes which questions we ask next.

r001.rationale: The response values new ways of thinking, but its example is connecting unrelated fields; it does not clearly express a preference for ideas originating from scratch over recombination.
